column1: bring up|/brɪŋ ʌp/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Introduce a topic into conversation, or raise a child.|Context immediately distinguishes introducing an idea from parenting.|I am glad you brought up parking logistics before we sent out the invitations.|mention,raise,broach~drop,ignore

come up with|/kʌm ʌp wɪð/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Invent, devise, or produce a clever idea, solution, or excuse.|Everyday powerhouse phrasal verb in creative and practical talk.|We need to come up with a rainy-day backup plan for Saturday's picnic.|devise,invent,produce~draw a blank

figure out|/ˈfɪɡjər aʊt/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Work through a puzzle or problem until you understand or solve it.|One of the most frequent American verbs for problem-solving.|It took twenty minutes, yet we finally figured out how to program the thermostat.|solve,work out,decode~stay baffled

work out|/wɜːrk aʊt/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Resolve successfully, calculate a detail, or exercise at the gym.|Three distinct everyday senses all anchored in steady effort.|Even though our flight shifted, the whole weekend itinerary worked out beautifully.|pan out,resolve,exercise~fall apart,fail

turn out|/tɜːrn aʊt/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|End up having a particular result, or attend an event in numbers.|Classic storytelling verb ('It turned out even better than expected').|Over two hundred neighbors turned out for the autumn lantern walk.|prove to be,result,attend~flop,stay home

end up|/ɛnd ʌp/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Eventually reach a situation or place, often unexpectedly.|Ubiquitous in American narrative speech.|We planned on quick tacos and ended up talking at the patio table for three hours.|wind up,finish up~start out

wind up|/waɪnd ʌp/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Ultimately arrive at a result—or bring a gathering or clock to a close.|Warm conversational cousin of end up (pronounced with a long 'i').|If we do not check the map soon, we will wind up halfway to the airport.|end up,conclude~begin,kick off

back up|/bæk ʌp/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Support a claim with evidence, make a data copy, or cause traffic congestion.|Triple-duty everyday American verb.|Always back up your travel photos to the cloud before deleting files from your phone.|support,copy,reverse~contradict,clear out

break down|/breɪk daʊn/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Stop working mechanically, analyze into clear parts, or become emotional.|Rich multi-sense verb essential for B2–C2 fluency.|Could you break down the lease utilities so each roommate sees their share?|analyze,fail,collapse~assemble,run smoothly

break into|/breɪk ˈɪntuː/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Successfully enter a competitive industry, or suddenly burst into laughter/song.|Also literally means burglarizing a building.|She spent two years freelancing before breaking into documentary editing.|enter,burst into~exit,stay out

break through|/breɪk θruː/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Overcome a stubborn barrier and achieve sudden progress or recognition.|Inspiring metaphor for science, art, and personal breakthroughs.|After months of plateauing, his conversational fluency finally broke through.|overcome,surge past~stall,hit a wall

bring about|/brɪŋ əˈbaʊt/|FORMAL|C1|Cause a significant change, reform, or outcome to happen.|Slightly more elevated than 'cause'; great for essays and discussions.|Neighborhood advocacy eventually brought about protected bike lanes along Main Street.|trigger,cause,spark~prevent,halt

bring back|/brɪŋ bæk/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Revive a nostalgic memory, trend, or discontinued favorite.|Warm, evocative everyday verb.|The smell of toasted cedar always brings back childhood summers at camp.|evoke,revive,restore~retire,erase

bring out|/brɪŋ aʊt/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Highlight someone's best traits, enhance a flavor, or launch a product.|Nuanced verb beloved in food, friendship, and design talk.|A pinch of flaky sea salt really brings out the sweetness in dark chocolate.|accentuate,reveal,release~hide,suppress

call off|/kɔːl ɔːf/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Cancel a scheduled event, match, or search.|Crisp, natural spoken alternative to 'cancel'.|Heavy lightning forced the park service to call off the evening kayak tour.|cancel,abort,scrap~go ahead with

call on|/kɔːl ɑːn/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Ask someone to speak, appeal to someone for help, or pay a brief visit.|Common in classrooms, meetings, and community appeals.|The city called on local restaurants to donate surplus bread to food pantries.|appeal to,ask,invite~bypass,ignore

carry on|/ˈkæri ɑːn/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Continue doing something steadily despite interruptions, or make a fuss.|Depending on tone, means either admirable grit or theatrical complaining.|Despite the brief power flicker, the string quartet calmly carried on playing.|continue,press on~halt,quit

carry out|/ˈkæri aʊt/|PROFESSIONAL|B2|Execute a detailed plan, study, promise, or inspection thoroughly.|Clean, polished phrasal verb for formal and workplace English.|Inspectors carried out a full safety review before reopening the footbridge.|execute,conduct,implement~abandon,neglect

catch on|/kætʃ ɑːn/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Gradually become widely popular, or suddenly understand a hint or rule.|Two very common everyday meanings.|It took me two rounds of the card game to catch on to the scoring rules.|grasp,become popular~miss the point,flop

check out of|/tʃɛk aʊt əv/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Officially depart a hotel, or mentally disengage from a boring situation.|Playful figurative use: 'mentally checked out by Friday afternoon'.|By three o'clock before a holiday weekend, half the room had mentally checked out.|sign out,disengage~check in,lock in

clear up|/klɪr ʌp/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Resolve a misunderstanding, improve weather, or heal a mild rash/cold.|Sunny, practical phrasal verb.|A quick five-minute phone call cleared up the scheduling confusion right away.|resolve,brighten,clarify~muddy,worsen

come across|/kʌm əˈkrɔːs/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Find something unexpectedly by chance, or leave a certain impression on others.|Watch both meanings: 'came across a vintage map' vs. 'comes across as warm'.|I came across a signed first edition while browsing that tiny basement bookshop.|stumble upon,seem,project~seek out,hide

come around|/kʌm əˈraʊnd/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Gradually change your mind and agree, or regain consciousness/visit again.|Common when stubborn skepticism softens into support.|Dad hated the idea of adopting a cat at first, yet he came around within a week.|relent,warm up to~dig in,refuse

come by|/kʌm baɪ/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Obtain something rare or tricky to find; also stop by casually.|Frequently heard in 'hard to come by'.|Truly quiet apartments with afternoon sunlight are hard to come by in Manhattan.|obtain,find,acquire~lose,give away

come down to|/kʌm daʊn tuː/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Boil down to one decisive core factor.|Essential framing verb for clear reasoning.|Ultimately, choosing between those two neighborhoods comes down to commute time.|boil down to,hinge on~branch out

come down with|/kʌm daʊn wɪð/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Begin showing symptoms of a mild contagious illness.|Natural everyday American alternative to 'contract a cold'.|I think I am coming down with a summer cold after sitting under that icy AC vent.|catch,develop~recover from

come forward|/kʌm ˈfɔːrwərd/|PROFESSIONAL|B2|Step up voluntarily to share information, witness testimony, or offer help.|Respectful verb common in journalism and community appeals.|Three local donors came forward to fund new instruments for the middle school band.|step up,volunteer~hang back,hide

come in handy|/kʌm ɪn ˈhændi/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Prove unexpectedly useful right when needed.|Classic practical American compliment for gear or skills.|Packing a pocket flashlight really came in handy when the cabin porch bulb blew.|prove useful,help out~sit unused

come off|/kʌm ɔːf/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Create a particular impression—or detach physically.|Closely related to come across ('She came off as genuinely confident').|Try to keep your tone warm so the written note does not come off as abrupt.|seem,appear,detach~project warmly

come out with|/kʌm aʊt wɪð/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Release a new album/product, or blurt out an unexpected remark.|Versatile spoken verb.|That independent studio just came out with a gorgeous hand-illustrated atlas.|release,launch,blurt out~retire,withhold

come over|/kʌm ˈoʊvər/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Visit someone's home casually, or (of a sudden feeling) overwhelm someone.|Everyday hospitality staple ('Come over anytime!').|Why don't you come over around six and we will grill peaches on the patio?|drop by,visit~head out

come through with|/kʌm θruː wɪð/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Deliver a promised favor, item, or support right when it matters.|Warm expression of gratitude.|Our local print shop came through with the festival posters two hours ahead of schedule.|deliver,provide~fall short on

come up against|/kʌm ʌp əˈɡɛnst/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Encounter unexpected resistance, tough competition, or a difficult hurdle.|Strong narrative verb for problem-solving stories.|The neighborhood mural project came up against unexpected historic-district zoning rules.|encounter,face,hit~sail past

count on|/kaʊnt ɑːn/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Rely confidently on someone's help or assume an outcome safely.|Expresses deep everyday trust.|You can always count on Devon to remember everyone's birthday without a calendar alert.|rely on,depend on~doubt,distrust

crack down on|/kræk daʊn ɑːn/|PROFESSIONAL|C1|Enforce rules much more strictly to stop abuses or violations.|Common in news, civic policy, and school/workplace governance.|The city is cracking down on double-parking along busy bus lanes.|clamp down on,enforce~turn a blind eye

crop up|/krɑːp ʌp/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Appear suddenly and unexpectedly, usually referring to minor tasks or issues.|Agricultural metaphor for sprouts popping up unannounced.|Two urgent client questions cropped up right before I closed my laptop.|pop up,arise,emerge~disappear,settle

cut back (on)|/kʌt bæk/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Intentionally reduce consumption, spending, or hours spent on something.|Healthy habit-change verb.|I have been cutting back on afternoon caffeine so I sleep more deeply.|reduce,scale back,trim~ramp up,increase

cut down (on)|/kʌt daʊn/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Lower the amount of something gradually to improve health or efficiency.|Interchangeable cousin of cut back on.|Switching to reusable glass jars cut down on our weekly kitchen waste dramatically.|trim,reduce,curb~increase,inflate

cut in|/kʌt ɪn/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Interrupt a conversation abruptly, or merge sharply in front of another car/person in line.|Generally carries mild annoyance unless politely prefaced.|Sorry to cut in, but the boarding agent just announced our final group.|interrupt,butt in~wait one's turn

cut off|/kʌt ɔːf/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Abruptly disconnect a call, interrupt mid-sentence, or swerve in front of traffic.|Common in driving, phone reception, and funding decisions.|My subway entered the tunnel and cut off our phone call right before the punchline.|disconnect,interrupt,block~connect,let finish

cut out for|/kʌt aʊt fɔːr/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Naturally suited by temperament or talent for a particular role.|Tailoring metaphor usually used in the negative ('not cut out for').|After one freezing ski trip, I realized I am simply not cut out for sub-zero sports.|suited for,built for~unsuited for

deal with|/diːl wɪð/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Handle a task, navigate a tough person, or cover a topic.|Workhorse American phrasal verb across every register.|I would rather deal with the insurance paperwork first thing Monday while I feel fresh.|handle,tackle,address~avoid,dodge

dig into|/dɪɡ ˈɪntuː/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Investigate a complex subject deeply—or start eating a delicious meal eagerly.|Warm dual meaning ('Dig in!' at dinner vs. 'dig into the archives').|Let's dig into the neighborhood history archives before writing our walking tour.|investigate,explore,eat eagerly~skim over

do away with|/duː əˈweɪ wɪð/|PROFESSIONAL|C1|Permanently abolish, eliminate, or retire an outdated rule or practice.|Crisp, articulate verb common in policy and design reviews.|The library finally did away with late fines to welcome back lapsed readers.|abolish,eliminate,scrap~introduce,keep

do over|/duː ˈoʊvər/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Repeat a task from scratch to fix a mistake (noun: 'a do-over').|Everyday American phrase for second chances.|The cake sank in the center, so I scraped the pan and did the whole batch over.|redo,repeat,remake~keep as is

do without|/duː wɪˈðaʊt/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Manage fine even when lacking something you normally enjoy.|Resilient everyday phrasing.|On a weekend camping trip, I can gladly do without phone reception for two days.|go without,forgo~rely on,need

drag on|/dræɡ ɑːn/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Continue tediously far longer than necessary or expected.|Vivid description for dull meetings, winter colds, or long flights.|A brief fifteen-minute check-in somehow dragged on for nearly two hours.|stretch out,linger~fly by,wrap up fast

draw on|/drɔː ɑːn/|PROFESSIONAL|C1|Tap into past experience, skills, or financial reserves as a resource.|Polished verb great for interviews and essays.|She drew on ten years of restaurant management when opening her community kitchen.|tap into,leverage,use~ignore,neglect

draw out|/drɔː aʊt/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Encourage a shy person to open up—or prolong something needlessly.|Context cleanly separates warm encouragement from 'drawn-out delays'.|A skilled podcast host knows how to draw out thoughtful stories from quiet guests.|elicit,prolong~cut short,silence

draw up|/drɔː ʌp/|PROFESSIONAL|C1|Draft a formal written plan, guest list, or legal contract.|Standard phrasing for leases, wills, and budgets.|Our attorney drew up a clear partnership agreement before we signed the studio lease.|draft,prepare,compose~tear up,scrap

drop off|/drɑːp ɔːf/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Deliver someone/something briefly, decline noticeably, or doze off to sleep.|Triple-duty everyday American verb.|Attendance usually drops off slightly in mid-August when families travel.|deliver,decline,doze off~pick up,surge

drop out (of)|/drɑːp aʊt/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Withdraw voluntarily from a course, race, or competition before finishing.|Neutral or candid verb depending on context.|An ankle strain forced two runners to drop out of the marathon at mile eighteen.|withdraw,quit,pull out~stick with,complete

ease up (on)|/iːz ʌp/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Become less intense (like rain or traffic), or go gentler on someone.|Relaxing, empathetic phrasal verb.|Let's wait five minutes under the awning until this heavy downpour eases up.|let up,lighten,soften~intensify,push harder

eat up|/iːt ʌp/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Consume time or money rapidly, or enjoy flattery/entertainment eagerly.|Vivid dual figurative verb ('The crowd ate up his jokes').|Unplanned bridge tolls and parking fees quickly ate up our weekend travel budget.|consume,devour,relish~save,reject

end up with|/ɛnd ʌp wɪð/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Finish a process holding a particular outcome or item, often unexpectedly.|Ubiquitous storytelling verb.|We went to the shelter for one senior cat and ended up with two bonded tabby brothers.|wind up with,finish with~start with

face up to|/feɪs ʌp tuː/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Courageously accept and confront an uncomfortable truth or responsibility.|Mature, reflective phrasal verb.|Eventually we had to face up to the fact that our twenty-year-old furnace needed replacing.|confront,accept,own up to~deny,dodge

fall apart|/fɔːl əˈpɑːrt/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Break physically into pieces, unravel structurally, or lose emotional composure.|Classic multi-purpose verb.|Without a clear agenda, the three-way negotiation quickly fell apart.|unravel,crumble,collapse~hold together,succeed

fall back on|/fɔːl bæk ɑːn/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Rely on a safe backup plan, savings, or skill when plan A fails.|Prudent planning verb.|Having an emergency fund gives freelancers a calm cushion to fall back on.|rely on,turn to~risk everything

fall behind|/fɔːl bɪˈhaɪnd/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Slip behind schedule, payments, or peers' pace.|Direct counterpart to catch up.|Missing two consecutive classes made it easy to fall behind on verb conjugations.|lag,slip back~keep up,pull ahead

fall for|/fɔːl fɔːr/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Be tricked by a prank or scam, or fall warmly in love with someone.|Context cleanly distinguishes romance from gullibility.|I cannot believe I fell for his April Fools' story about a rooftop penguin exhibit.|get fooled by,fall in love with~see through,resist

fall out (with)|/fɔːl aʊt/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Have a serious argument that damages a friendship (noun: 'a falling-out').|Also describes hair or loose items dropping out.|They had a brief falling-out over moving costs, though they patched things up months later.|quarrel,break off~make up,reconcile

fend off|/fɛnd ɔːf/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Successfully ward off an attack, unwanted questions, or a looming cold.|Energetic defensive phrasal verb.|Hot ginger tea and early sleep helped me fend off the winter flu making rounds.|ward off,repel,deflect~succumb to,welcome

fill in (for)|/fɪl ɪn/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Temporarily cover someone's shift, role, or duties while they are away.|Everyday teamwork verb distinct from 'fill someone in' (update).|Could you fill in for me at the front desk while I grab lunch for fifteen minutes?|cover for,sub for~leave uncovered

fill out|/fɪl aʊt/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Complete every blank field on a form or application.|Standard American preference (UK often says 'fill in a form').|Please fill out the emergency contact form before your first climbing class.|complete,enter~leave blank

find out|/faɪnd aʊt/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Discover a fact, secret, or answer after checking or hearing news.|Everyday conversational staple.|Let me call the ferry terminal to find out whether bikes need separate tickets.|discover,learn,uncover~stay oblivious

fit in|/fɪt ɪn/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Feel socially accepted within a group, or squeeze a quick appointment into a packed schedule.|Two super-common everyday senses.|Even on a packed Tuesday, my dentist managed to fit me in for a quick check.|belong,squeeze in~stick out,miss out

fix up|/fɪks ʌp/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Repair, renovate, or stylishly refresh an old house, car, or room.|Also means setting two friends up on a blind date.|They bought a 1950s cottage and spent two summers fixing it up themselves.|renovate,restore,spruce up~neglect,wreck

follow up (on)|/ˈfɑːloʊ ʌp/|PROFESSIONAL|B2|Check back after an initial email, lead, or repair to make sure it progresses.|Cornerstone American workplace and everyday habit.|I will follow up with the landlord Thursday if we have not heard back about the lease.|check back,pursue~drop,forget

freak someone out|/friːk ˈsʌmwʌn aʊt/|CASUAL|B2|Startle, unsettle, or creep someone out unexpectedly.|Expressive casual transitive verb.|Walking into a dark cabin and hearing an owl hoot right above the roof freaked me out.|spook,unsettle,alarm~reassure,calm

freshen up|/ˈfrɛʃən ʌp/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Wash your face, tidy up after travel, or add fresh paint/drinks.|Polite everyday phrase when welcoming travelers.|Make yourself at home and take a few minutes to freshen up after that long flight.|tidy up,refresh~stay dusty

get across|/ɡɛt əˈkrɔːs/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Communicate a complex idea clearly so listeners genuinely grasp it.|Essential speaking and writing goal.|A single real-world dialogue gets the nuance across far faster than three grammar rules.|convey,communicate,express~muddy,confuse

get ahead|/ɡɛt əˈhɛd/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Make meaningful upward progress in a career, savings, or schedule.|Core American aspiration verb.|Knocking out errands Friday afternoon helps you get ahead before the weekend rush.|advance,progress~fall behind,stall

get along (with)|/ɡɛt əˈlɔːŋ/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Enjoy a harmonious, friendly relationship with someone.|Everyday measure of roommate, family, and team chemistry.|Our golden retriever somehow gets along famously with the grumpy neighborhood cat.|bond,mesh,click~clash,feud

get around|/ɡɛt əˈraʊnd/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Travel easily around a city, bypass a restriction, or spread quickly like news.|Versatile three-sense phrasal verb.|With the new tram extension, getting around Portland without a car is effortless.|navigate,bypass,spread~get stuck

get around to|/ɡɛt əˈraʊnd tuː/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Finally find the time to tackle a long-postponed chore.|Relatable everyday confession verb.|I keep meaning to organize the closet, yet I never quite get around to it.|find time for,tackle~keep putting off

get away with|/ɡɛt əˈweɪ wɪð/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Escape punishment or criticism for bending a rule or taking a risk.|Used both seriously and playfully.|You can usually get away with wearing clean sneakers to creative agency meetings.|escape penalty,pull off~get caught,pay for

get back at|/ɡɛt bæk æt/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Retaliate playfully or spitefully against someone who wronged you.|Common in sibling prank stories and dramas.|He got back at his brother for the salt-in-coffee prank by hiding every left shoe.|retaliate,pay back~forgive,let go

get back to|/ɡɛt bæk tuː/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Reply to someone once you have checked details, or return to a paused topic.|Essential polite office and texting phrase.|Let me confirm the flight window with Sam and get back to you before five.|reply,follow up~ghost,forget

get by|/ɡɛt baɪ/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Manage to survive or communicate adequately with modest resources or skill.|Humility-filled verb common in languages and budgets.|My spoken Italian is basic, though I know enough phrases to get by at local markets.|manage,scrape by,cope~thrive,struggle badly

get carried away|/ɡɛt ˈkærid əˈweɪ/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Become so excited that you overdo something beyond your original plan.|Affectionate self-critique during shopping, cooking, or decorating.|I went to the nursery for one basil plant and got carried away buying six herbs.|overdo it,go overboard~hold back,stay moderate

get down to|/ɡɛt daʊn tuː/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Stop chatting casually and begin serious focused work.|Brisk transition verb ('Let's get down to business').|Now that everyone has coffee, let's get down to mapping out our summer route.|focus on,tackle~stall,chat around

get into|/ɡɛt ˈɪntuː/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Develop a genuine passion for a new hobby, get accepted to a school, or start an argument.|Ultra-common everyday verb.|Ever since last winter, Maya has really gotten into film photography.|develop interest in,enter~lose interest in

get over|/ɡɛt ˈoʊvər/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Recover emotionally from a setback or illness, or overcome disbelief.|Double meaning: 'get over a cold' vs. 'I can't get over how cozy this loft is!'.|It took a full week of herbal tea to finally get over that stubborn autumn cold.|recover from,move past~dwell on,linger

get through|/ɡɛt θruː/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Endure a tough stretch, reach someone by phone, or make someone understand.|Workhorse three-sense American phrasal verb.|Checking in daily with friends helped all of us get through that icy winter.|endure,connect,reach~give up,disconnect

get together|/ɡɛt təˈɡɛðər/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Meet up socially as friends or family (noun: 'a get-together').|Warm, relaxed everyday hospitality phrase.|We should get together for dim sum before you fly back to Seattle.|meet up,gather~cancel,stay apart

give away|/ɡɪv əˈweɪ/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Donate for free, accidentally spoil a secret/ending, or reveal a hidden tell.|Watch both generosity and accidental spoilers.|Please don't give away the mystery novel's ending—I only have twenty pages left!|donate,reveal,spoil~keep,conceal

give back|/ɡɪv bæk/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Contribute time or support to a community that helped you, or return an item.|Deeply valued American civic phrase.|Coaching weekend youth soccer is her favorite way to give back to the neighborhood.|contribute,repay~take only

give off|/ɡɪv ɔːf/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Emit a scent, warmth, light, or subtle emotional vibe.|Sensory and social verb ('gives off a welcoming energy').|The pine candles give off a subtle woodsy scent without feeling overpowering.|emit,radiate,project~absorb,conceal

give out|/ɡɪv aʊt/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Distribute items to a crowd, run empty, or fail mechanically/physically.|Useful for aging knees, batteries, and handouts alike.|My old running shoes finally gave out right at the end of spring training.|distribute,fail,run out~hold up,collect

give up on|/ɡɪv ʌp ɑːn/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Stop believing in or trying to rescue someone or something.|Emotionally clear everyday phrase.|Never give up on a language after a tough week—consistency always wins.|abandon,write off~stick with,believe in

go after|/ɡoʊ ˈæftər/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Pursue an ambitious goal boldly—or criticize/chase someone aggressively.|Context signals ambition ('go after that fellowship') versus hostility.|If that urban-planning grant excites you, go after it with everything you have.|pursue,chase~pass up,avoid

go ahead|/ɡoʊ əˈhɛd/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Proceed with permission, or start eating/speaking without waiting.|Ubiquitous polite American invitation ('Go right ahead!').|Go ahead and start the movie—I will join you as soon as the popcorn pops.|proceed,carry on~hold off,wait

go along with|/ɡoʊ əˈlɔːŋ wɪð/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Agree to support or play along with someone's idea or harmless joke.|Flexible everyday verb for cooperation.|I went along with the surprise detour even though I had no clue where we were driving.|agree to,play along~push back,oppose

go back on|/ɡoʊ bæk ɑːn/|CONVERSATIONAL|C1|Break a solemn promise, word, or earlier agreement.|Carries strong moral disappointment.|A dependable contractor never goes back on a signed price quote.|renege on,break~honor,keep

go by|/ɡoʊ baɪ/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Pass quickly (time), use a preferred nickname, or judge based on evidence.|Triple-duty everyday verb ('Her name is Katherine, though she goes by Kate').|Wait—did three whole hours really go by while we painted the porch?|elapse,use name,judge by~drag on

go down|/ɡoʊ daʊn/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Decrease, happen ('What's going down?'), fail (a server), or be remembered in history.|Rich multi-sense everyday verb.|That overtime comeback will go down as the greatest match our city ever hosted.|drop,occur,crash~rise,stay up

go for|/ɡoʊ fɔːr/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Enthusiastically choose, crave, or encourage someone boldly ('Go for it!').|Upbeat everyday slang ('I could really go for iced tea right now').|You have practiced that audition piece for weeks—step up and go for it!|choose,crave,attempt~pass on,hesitate

go off|/ɡoʊ ɔːf/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Ring loudly (alarm), explode, spoil (milk), or suddenly start ranting enthusiastically.|Everyday verb with vivid spoken nuances.|My travel alarm went off at four-thirty, yet the sunrise hike was worth it.|ring,detonate,rant~stay silent

go on|/ɡoʊ ɑːn/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Continue speaking, take place, or gently encourage someone ('Go on, tell me!').|Core conversational cue.|Sorry for the brief interruption—please go on with your story about Lisbon.|continue,happen~stop,pause

go out of one's way|/ɡoʊ aʊt əv wʌnz weɪ/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Make a special thoughtful detour or extra effort to help someone.|Warm gratitude phrase for hospitality and kindness.|Our Airbnb host went out of her way to leave handwritten neighborhood café maps.|take extra trouble~do bare minimum

go over|/ɡoʊ ˈoʊvər/|CONVERSATIONAL|B2|Review carefully step-by-step, or receive a specific audience reaction.|Context distinguishes 'go over the checklist' from 'went over great'.|Let's go over the packing checklist once more before locking the trunk.|review,check,be received~skip,gloss over
